title: Static Storage and the Layout of a Program in Memory
summary: Besides the stack and the heap, a running program has memory that exists for its whole life: its **code**, its **constants** and its **global and static variables**. These come straight from the `.exe` file, in named **sections**. Knowing the layout tells you at a glance what kind of thing an address points to.
markdown:
## Three kinds of storage Every object in a C++ program has a **storage duration**: how long its memory exists. | Storage duration | Examples | Lives | Memory comes from | |---|---|---|---| | **Automatic** | Locals, function arguments | Until the block or function ends | The stack | | **Dynamic** | Anything from `new`, containers' contents | Until freed | The heap | | **Static** | Globals, `static` variables, string literals | The whole run of the program | The program's own image | The last row is this lesson's subject. Static storage is not allocated while the program runs at all. It is laid out by the compiler and linker, written into the `.exe` file, and mapped into memory by the loader before `main` starts. ## Sections of an executable The linker groups everything with static storage into **sections**, each with its own purpose and its own memory protection. | Section | Holds | Protection when loaded | |---|---|---| | `.text` | The machine code of every function | Read and execute | | `.rdata` | Read-only data: string literals, `const` globals, tables the compiler generates | Read only | | `.data` | Global and static variables that start with a value | Read and write | | `.bss` part of `.data` | Globals that start at zero. They take no room in the file, only in memory | Read and write | | `.pdata`, `.reloc`, `.idata` ... | Bookkeeping for exceptions, relocation and imports | Read only | The protections are enforced by the processor, page by page. Writing to `.rdata` or `.text` crashes the program with an **access violation**. Chapter 6 explains page protection, and chapter 9 reads these sections straight out of an `.exe`. ```cpp #include int g_highScore{ 1200 }; // .data: starts with a value, can change int g_frameCount; // zero-initialised: takes no space in the .exe file const int g_maxLives{ 3 }; // .rdata (or folded straight into the code) const char* g_title{ "Dungeon" }; // the pointer is in .data; the characters are in .rdata int nextId() { static int counter{ 0 }; // static local: lives in .data, initialised once return ++counter; } int main() { std::cout << nextId() << ' ' << nextId() << ' ' << nextId() << '\n'; std::cout << g_highScore << ' ' << g_frameCount << ' ' << g_maxLives << ' ' << g_title << '\n'; return 0; } ``` ``` 1 2 3 1200 0 3 Dungeon ``` The `static` local `counter` behaves like a global with a private name. It is initialised once, the first time `nextId` runs, and keeps its value between calls because it is not in any stack frame. ## The whole picture Put the three kinds of storage together and you have the outline of a process's memory. On 64-bit Windows the exact addresses are randomised (lesson 6.09), but the families are recognisable: ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph IMG["The program's image (static storage)"] T[".text: code"] R[".rdata: constants, string literals"] D[".data: globals and statics"] end H["Heap blocks
(new, vector, string)"] S["Stack
(one per thread)"] DLL["DLL images: kernel32, the C++ runtime, ...
each with their own .text, .rdata, .data"] ``` You can see the families by printing one address of each kind: ```cpp #include #include int g_global{ 7 }; void someFunction() {} int main() { int local{ 1 }; auto onHeap{ std::make_unique(2) }; static int staticLocal{ 3 }; std::cout << "code " << reinterpret_cast(&someFunction) << '\n'; std::cout << "literal " << static_cast("hello") << '\n'; std::cout << "global " << &g_global << '\n'; std::cout << "static " << &staticLocal << '\n'; std::cout << "heap " << onHeap.get() << '\n'; std::cout << "stack " << &local << '\n'; return 0; } ``` ```varies code 00007FF7A3E413B6 literal 00007FF7A3E5AC28 global 00007FF7A3E61000 static 00007FF7A3E61004 heap 0000020E6C8F5E30 stack 000000E4F1CFF6A4 ``` Look at the first four. They share most of their digits (`00007FF7A3E...`), because code, literals and globals are all parts of the same image, loaded as one block. Within it, code comes first, then read-only data, then writable data. The heap and the stack are somewhere else entirely, and each looks different. With a little practice you can tell what a pointer points at from its value alone: a very useful skill in the Memory window. ## Initialisation order, and why globals are risky Globals with simple constant initial values are written straight into the `.data` section by the linker, so they are ready before any code runs. Globals that need code to initialise them (a `std::string`, a `std::vector`, anything with a constructor) run that code before `main`, in an order that is only defined **within one `.cpp` file**. Across files, the order is unspecified. A global in `a.cpp` that uses a global from `b.cpp` during its own initialisation may see it not yet constructed. This is called the **static initialisation order fiasco**. The usual fix is the pattern `nextId` used: a function holding a `static` local. The local is initialised the first time the function is called, whatever order things happen in, and C++ guarantees this is safe even with threads. ```cpp #include const std::string& defaultPlayerName() { static const std::string name{ "Adventurer" }; // built on first use, then kept return name; } ``` More generally, mutable globals make code hard to follow and hard to test, because any function might change them. Use them sparingly. Constants are fine. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Writing through a pointer to a string literal > `char* s = (char*)"hello"; s[0] = 'J';` crashes: the characters are in read-only `.rdata`. Copy the text into a `std::string` or a `char` array first. > [!warning] Returning a pointer to a static buffer > A function that fills a `static char buffer[64]` and returns it hands every caller the same buffer, so the second call overwrites what the first caller still holds. It is also unsafe with threads. > [!warning] Assuming globals in different files are initialised in a particular order > They are not. Use a function with a `static` local for anything that other globals depend on. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What are the three storage durations, and where does each one's memory come from? - Local (registers), global (the heap), constant (the stack) - Automatic (the heap), dynamic (the stack), static (the registers) - Short (the stack), long (the disk), permanent (the program image) + Automatic (the stack), dynamic (the heap), static (the program's image, laid out by the linker) > Static storage is laid out by the linker and mapped in by the loader, so it exists for the whole run of the program. ? What is the difference between `.data` and `.rdata`? - `.data` holds code; `.rdata` holds variables + `.data` holds writable globals that start with a value; `.rdata` holds read-only data such as string literals - `.data` holds zero-initialised globals; `.rdata` holds everything else - `.rdata` is copied into `.data` when the program starts > Writing to `.rdata` crashes. Zero-initialised globals go in `.bss`, which takes no space in the file. ? How does a function with a `static` local avoid initialisation-order problems? + The local is initialised the first time the function is called, so it is ready whenever anything uses it - The local is initialised before `main` along with all other globals - The compiler sorts all statics so they are initialised in the right order > The order in which globals in different files are set up is not fixed, but a function's `static` local is set up on first use, whatever that order was. ? Which section holds the characters of the string literal `"Game Over"`? - `.text` + `.rdata` - `.data` > Literals are read-only data. Writing to them is an access violation. ? A `static int counter{ 0 };` inside a function. How many times is `counter` initialised? + Once, the first time the function runs - Every time the function is called - Never: statics are always zero > A static local lives in static storage for the whole program and is initialised the first time control reaches its declaration. ? Two addresses are `00007FF6C1A21000` and `00007FF6C1A3B0E0`. What is the most likely relationship? - One is on the stack and one is on the heap + Both are inside the same loaded image, such as the `.exe` - They belong to two different processes > They share their high digits and differ only in the low ones: about 100 KB apart, typical of sections within one module. ? Why does a zero-initialised global array of a million `int`s not make the `.exe` four megabytes bigger? - The compiler compresses it + Zeroed data takes no file space; the loader supplies zeroes - Globals are always allocated on the heap > The file only records how much zeroed memory is needed, not the zeros themselves. ```
ideas:
- Run the address example several times. Which addresses change from run to run, and which parts stay similar?
- Add a second global and a second string literal and see where their addresses fall.
- In Visual Studio, open **Debug → Windows → Modules** while paused. Find your program in the list: the address range it shows contains the code, literal, global and static addresses you printed.

cards.q: What are the three storage durations, and where does each one's memory come from?
cards.a:
Automatic (the stack), dynamic (the heap), static (the program's image, laid out by the linker)

Static storage is laid out by the linker and mapped in by the loader, so it exists for the whole run of the program.

cards.q: What is the difference between `.data` and `.rdata`?
cards.a:
`.data` holds writable globals that start with a value; `.rdata` holds read-only data such as string literals

Writing to `.rdata` crashes. Zero-initialised globals go in `.bss`, which takes no space in the file.

cards.q: How does a function with a `static` local avoid initialisation-order problems?
cards.a:
The local is initialised the first time the function is called, so it is ready whenever anything uses it

The order in which globals in different files are set up is not fixed, but a function's `static` local is set up on first use, whatever that order was.

cards.q: Which section holds the characters of the string literal `"Game Over"`?
cards.a:
`.rdata`

Literals are read-only data. Writing to them is an access violation.

cards.q: A `static int counter{ 0 };` inside a function. How many times is `counter` initialised?
cards.a:
Once, the first time the function runs

A static local lives in static storage for the whole program and is initialised the first time control reaches its declaration.

cards.q: Two addresses are `00007FF6C1A21000` and `00007FF6C1A3B0E0`. What is the most likely relationship?
cards.a:
Both are inside the same loaded image, such as the `.exe`

They share their high digits and differ only in the low ones: about 100 KB apart, typical of sections within one module.

cards.q: Why does a zero-initialised global array of a million `int`s not make the `.exe` four megabytes bigger?
cards.a:
Zeroed data takes no file space; the loader supplies zeroes

The file only records how much zeroed memory is needed, not the zeros themselves.
